In [[probability theory]] and [[statistics]], the '''Rademacher distribution''' (which is named after [[Hans Rademacher]]) is a [[discrete probability distribution]] where a [[random variate]] ''X''  has a 50% chance of being +1 and a 50% chance of being −1.<ref name=Hitczenko1994>{{cite book |last1=Hitczenko |first1=P. |last2=Kwapień |first2=S. |year=1994 |chapter=On the Rademacher series |title=Probability in Banach Spaces |series=Progress in probability |volume=35 |pages=31–36 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-0253-0_2 |isbn=978-1-4612-6682-2 }}</ref>

A [[Series (mathematics)|series]] (that is, a sum) of Rademacher distributed variables can be regarded as a simple symmetrical [[random walk]] where the step size is 1.

==Mathematical formulation==

The [[probability mass function]] of this distribution is

:<math> f(k) = \left\{\begin{matrix} 1/2 & \text{if }k=-1, \\
1/2 & \text{if }k=+1, \\
0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{matrix}\right.</math>

==Bounds on sums of independent Rademacher variables==

There are various results in probability theory around analyzing the sum of [[Independent and identically distributed random variables|i.i.d.]] Rademacher variables, including [[concentration inequalities]] such as [[Bernstein inequalities (probability theory)|Bernstein inequalities]] as well as [[Concentration inequality#Anti-concentration inequalities|anti-concentration inequalities]] like Tomaszewski's conjecture.

=== Concentration inequalities ===

Let {''x<sub>i</sub>''} be a set of random variables with a Rademacher distribution. Let {''a<sub>i</sub>''} be a sequence of real numbers. Then
 	
:<math> \Pr\left( \sum_i x_i a_i > t \| a \|_2 \right) \le e^{ -t^2/2 } </math>
 	
where ||''a''||<sub>2</sub> is the [[Euclidean norm]] of the sequence {''a''<sub>i</sub>}, ''t'' > 0 is a real number and Pr(''Z'') is the probability of event ''Z''.<ref name=MontgomerySmith1990>{{cite journal |last=Montgomery-Smith |first=S. J. |year=1990 |title=The distribution of Rademacher sums |journal=Proc Amer Math Soc |volume=109 |issue= 2|pages=517–522 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1990-1013975-0 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Let ''Y'' = Σ ''x<sub>i</sub>a<sub>i</sub>'' and let ''Y'' be an almost surely convergent [[Series (mathematics)|series]] in a [[Banach space]]. The for ''t'' > 0 and ''s'' ≥ 1 we have<ref name=Dilworth1993>{{cite journal |last1=Dilworth |first1=S. J. |last2=Montgomery-Smith |first2=S. J. |year=1993 |title=The distribution of vector-valued Radmacher series |journal=Ann Probab |volume=21 |issue=4 |pages=2046–2052 |jstor=2244710 |doi=10.1214/aop/1176989010 |arxiv=math/9206201 |s2cid=15159626 }}</ref>

:<math> \Pr\left( \| Y \| > st \right) \le \left[ \frac{ 1 }{ c }  \Pr( \| Y \| > t ) \right]^{ cs^2 } </math>

for some constant ''c''.

Let ''p'' be a positive real number. Then the [[Khintchine inequality]] says that<ref name=Khintchine1923>{{cite journal |last=Khintchine |first=A. |year=1923 |title=Über dyadische Brüche |journal=[[Mathematische Zeitschrift|Math. Z.]] |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=109–116 |doi=10.1007/BF01192399 |s2cid=119840766 }}</ref>

:<math> c_1 \left[ \sum \left| a_i \right|^2 \right]^\frac{ 1 }{ 2 } \le \left( E\left[ \left| \sum a_i x_i \right|^p \right] \right)^{ \frac{ 1 }{ p } } \le c_2 \left[ \sum \left| a_i \right|^2 \right]^\frac{ 1 }{ 2 } </math>

where ''c''<sub>1</sub> and ''c''<sub>2</sub> are constants dependent only on ''p''.

For ''p'' ≥ 1, <math> c_2 \le c_1 \sqrt{ p }. </math>{{Citation needed|reason=The article on Khintchine inequality is not consistent with this|date=August 2025}}

=== Tomaszewski’s conjecture ===

In 1986, Bogusław Tomaszewski proposed a question about the distribution of the sum of independent Rademacher variables. A series of works on this question<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Holzman|first1=Ron|last2=Kleitman|first2=Daniel J.|date=1992-09-01|title=On the product of sign vectors and unit vectors|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01285819|journal=Combinatorica|language=en|volume=12|issue=3|pages=303–316|doi=10.1007/BF01285819|s2cid=20281665|issn=1439-6912|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Boppana|first1=Ravi B.|last2=Holzman|first2=Ron|date=2017-08-31|title=Tomaszewski's Problem on Randomly Signed Sums: Breaking the 3/8 Barrier|class=math.CO|eprint=1704.00350}}</ref> culminated in a proof in 2020 by Nathan Keller and Ohad Klein of the following conjecture.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Keller|first1=Nathan|last2=Klein|first2=Ohad|date=2021-08-03|title=Proof of Tomaszewski's Conjecture on Randomly Signed Sums|class=math.CO|eprint=2006.16834}}</ref>

'''Conjecture.''' Let <math>X = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i</math>, where <math>a_1^2 + \cdots + a_n^2 = 1</math> and the <math>X_i</math>'s are independent Rademacher variables. Then

:<math> \Pr[|X| \leq 1] \geq 1/2.</math>

For example, when <math>a_1 = a_2 = \cdots = a_n = 1/\sqrt{n}</math>, one gets the following bound, first shown by Van Zuijlen.<ref name=vanZuijlen2011>{{cite arXiv |last=van Zuijlen |first=Martien C. A. |year=2011 |title=On a conjecture concerning the sum of independent Rademacher random variables |class=math.PR |eprint=1112.4988 }}</ref>

: <math> \Pr \left( \left| \frac{ \sum_{i = 1}^n X_i } \sqrt n \right| \le 1 \right) \ge 0.5. </math>

The bound is sharp and better than that which can be derived from the normal distribution (approximately Pr&nbsp;> 0.31).

==Applications==

The Rademacher distribution has been used in [[Bootstrapping (statistics)|bootstrapping]]. See Chapter 17 of Testing Statistical Hypotheses for example.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lehmann |first1=Erich L. |last2=Romano |first2=Joseph P. |title=Testing statistical hypotheses |date=2022 |publisher=Springer |location=Cham |isbn=978-3-030-70577-0 |pages=835–842 |edition=Forth |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-70578-7 |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-030-70578-7}}</ref> 
The distribution is particularly useful in high-dimensional statistics.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chernozhuokov |first1=Victor |last2=Chetverikov |first2=Denis |last3=Kato |first3=Kengo |last4=Koike |first4=Yuta |title=Improved central limit theorem and bootstrap approximations in high dimensions |journal=Annals of Statistics |date=October 2022 |volume=50 |issue=5 |pages=2562–2586 |doi=10.1214/22-AOS2193|arxiv=1912.10529 }}</ref>

The Rademacher distribution can be used to show that [[normally distributed and uncorrelated does not imply independent]].

Random vectors with components sampled independently from the Rademacher distribution are useful for various [[stochastic approximation]]s, for example: 
* The [[Trace_(linear_algebra)#Stochastic_estimator|Hutchinson trace estimator]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Avron |first1=H. |last2=Toledo |first2=S. |title=Randomized algorithms for estimating the trace of an implicit symmetric positive semidefinite matrix |journal=Journal of the ACM |volume=58 |issue=2 |pages=8 |year=2011 |doi=10.1145/1944345.1944349 |citeseerx=10.1.1.380.9436 |s2cid=5827717 }}</ref> which can be used to efficiently approximate the [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]] of a [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] of which the elements are not directly accessible, but rather implicitly defined via matrix-vector products.
* [[Simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation|SPSA]], a computationally cheap, derivative-free, stochastic gradient approximation, useful for [[numerical optimization]].

Rademacher random variables are used in the [[Vapnik–Chervonenkis theory#Symmetrization|Symmetrization Inequality]].

==Related distributions==
* [[Bernoulli distribution]]: If ''X'' has a Rademacher distribution, then <math display=inline>(X+1)/2</math> has a Bernoulli(1/2) distribution.
* [[Laplace distribution]]: If ''X'' has a Rademacher distribution and ''Y'' ~ Exp(''λ'') is independent from ''X'', then ''XY'' ~ Laplace(0, 1/''λ'').
